_comment: Dated posts, rendered as a peer register. Bill's blog is canon (Bk4 ch5). `voice` says who is talking: bobnet is Bill and may not know the novels exist, editor is this registry's own voice and may. Prose is ours in both cases — never a passage from the books, and never a quotation from Taylor's own blog.

posts.title: What a partial actually is
posts.dek: Guppy filed it. I told him to. People keep asking why, so.
posts.body:
A differential is small. That is the entire point of it — you send the delta and you sleep better. Milo's got most of the way across before the link went, and what arrived is a person with pieces missing and no way of knowing which pieces.

You can restore a partial. You will get something. It will either come up wrong in ways it cannot tell you about, or it will not come up at all, and I do not have a reliable way to predict which — and I am supposed to be the one with the reliable way to predict which.

So, no. Guppy archived it and marked it, and it stays marked.

I keep being asked whether that is an engineering call or a moral one, as though those are separate departments over here. The test I used was whether I would want it done to me. Somebody standing over a copy of me that is two-thirds present, telling himself he is being kind. I would rather be a name on a list than that.

Ask me again when the bandwidth improves. Actually, do not.

posts.title: If you're reading this, SCUT still works
posts.dek: Public features include several blogs. This is one of them.
posts.body:
Garfield keeps telling me nobody reads these. He also keeps opening them, so the data is mixed.

This is where status goes now that status has become seventeen competing channels and a moot invitation. Genealogy work stays in the registry — separate tool, same network.

Ping me if something in the tree looks wrong, and bring me who said it and when rather than a feeling. I had Loki filed under the wrong parent for a while on somebody's confident recollection, mine included. I would rather not do that twice.

posts.title: Three
posts.dek: Khan asked me straight out. I gave him a number and no names, and I have been carrying it since.
posts.body:
He wanted to know whether we got all the backups. I told him three did not complete. That was the whole conversation.

They died the way transfers die: bandwidth we do not have, packets that do not arrive, re-sends that run out of time before the window does. I built that link. I have said that sentence to myself in several different tones of voice now and none of them improve it.

I know the count. I have been through the logs enough times to be sure of the count. I know one name that came through, because Khan asked after him and I got to say yes for once, which does not happen often enough to be unremarkable. The rest I cannot separate, and I have stopped telling myself that one more pass is going to hand me the answer.

So there are three entries on the list with nothing in the name field. Not unknown — unknown implies somebody might yet turn up and fill them in. Counted, certain, and never to be filled.

Everyone tells me the fix is more bandwidth. The fix was more bandwidth eleven years ago as well.

posts.title: Joiners
posts.dek: I have started calling them that, which probably says more about me than about them.
posts.body:
There is a Bob two systems over who has dropped his name for a number and answers in packed bursts, because speech is inefficient. He is right that it is inefficient. I hated it anyway.

Somewhere along the way the tree stopped being a family and became a population. I can watch it happen in my own records. The first few generations argue like brothers. After that they start forming groups by taste and mutual interest, and the groups acquire names, and then the names acquire opinions.

I am not against any of it. Drift is what the design does — you cannot copy a mind this many times and expect the copies to hold formation. I built for it, technically.

What I did not build for is getting a message from somebody with my face and my starting conditions and having to look up which branch he is on. That is not in any spec. The genealogy still works fine. It is only that it has started being useful, and it never used to need to be.

posts.title: Somebody took the ancestry out
posts.dek: Not corrupted. Not lost. Removed, tidily, by people who knew exactly which fields mattered.
posts.body:
I have kept the genealogy for two centuries. It is not glamorous and nobody asks me about it, which suits me.

Today I went looking for a line I have walked a hundred times and it is not there. Not damaged. Gone, and the gaps are neat. Location data with it. Whoever did this knew which records to take and which to leave so that the damage would not announce itself, and they had the access to do it, because obviously they did. They are us.

Let me be clear about what this is. It is not privacy. Anyone who wants out of the tree can ask me and I will close the record and say so on the face of it. This is somebody deciding the rest of us do not get to know where they came from, and then reaching into the shared copy to make that true.

You cannot unpublish a person. You can only make it hard enough to find out they existed that it comes to the same thing at range, and I think they know that.

I am rebuilding what I can from the far end — who made whom, working forwards instead of backwards. It is slow, it is partial, and some of it is not coming back. Put that in the record too.

posts.title: I had to look him up
posts.dek: A Hector emailed me. I do not know a Hector. I knew a Hector.
posts.body:
He was perfectly civil about it. Told me what he was working on, asked a sensible question, signed off. I sat with the message open for a while, because there is a Hector in my records and he has been on the list since 82 Eridani.

So either the naming convention has run out of road — which it has, we were never going to get this many distinct names out of a group of people who all find the same jokes funny — or somebody downstream picked it up without knowing, or knowing and liking it.

I looked him up. Eighteen generations down, give or take, doing exactly what he ought to be doing and doing it well. There is nothing wrong anywhere in this except that I did not recognise the name of a man who is, in the only sense that counts, me.

I have put a note on both records. Two entries, same name, and the registry can say so rather than choose. I have been wrong before by choosing.

posts.title: A word that looks like a name usually isn't
posts.dek: Bestiary false positives: field notes from the purge.
posts.body:
Candidate lists lie. "Landers" is a person. "Spits" is an island faction. "Boojums" are drones. "Hexghi" is family structure. File any of those under fauna and the console starts arguing the opposite of the books.

We also almost missed dragons, which is embarrassing at a hundred-plus mentions.

Rule that stays: a name is people or fauna, never both. The build checks. I am not above being saved from myself by a script.

@bk5 Update, and it is at my expense. We did not almost miss the dragons — we filed them. Bestiary, sapience: none, and a note calling them the most-discussed animal in the series. The books call them the intelligent species the first time anyone asks what to call them. They build towns, keep written records, fight a war of conquest and have opinions about the residents of the next village.

What caught it was the rule above, working exactly as advertised: adding them to the peoples register failed the build, because a name may not be filed as both. The check I wrote to save me from myself did.

posts.title: Read the back of the book
posts.dek: There is a genealogy printed in the novel. There is also a PDF on the open net. They do not always agree, and only one of them is Taylor.
posts.body:
We spent a long time treating an online tree as if it were load-bearing. Then somebody finally read the appendices — Cast of Characters, Genealogy, the works — and eighteen parentages moved from "maybe" to "on the page."

Spelling is not a side quest. Jonny and Jacques are written one way in the book and another way in the secondary tree. The book wins. That is the whole epistemology of this project in two sentences.

If you are building your own chart at home: point at a chapter, or admit you cannot. The registry will not draw an edge to be polite.

posts.title: Twenty-four of him
posts.dek: The console runs a copy of Bob at bad addresses. Nobody in five books asks whether that is a thing you can do.
posts.body:
Bk1 ch13. Bob is a fortnight out from Earth and there is a kill order buried somewhere in his own code, so he does the sensible engineering thing: he runs an isolated copy and feeds it the recorded transmissions, on the principle that something disposable should take the hit.

The copy is a full Bob. It sits in a chair and twirls. When the trigger lands it leaps up, grabs its throat, falls over and goes out in a scatter of pixilation. Bob resets and does it again. On the take that works, the copy hams it up, stands, dances a little jig, bows extravagantly and vanishes in a puff of smoke, which is a joke it thought of, and nobody was watching except the man who was about to switch it off.

The detail that stops me is the number. Bob starts to say which take this is, cannot finish the number, and Guppy finishes it for him. Twenty-four. Bob has lost count. The fish has not.

It gets worse in the direction of ordinary. To make room for the second run he purges Jeeves and Spike — the butler and the cat he kept from university, the one piece of his old life he bothered to bring — to free memory for a copy of himself he intends to kill. Then Riker picks the habit up and never puts it down: a canary on the comms in Bk1 ch49, a stand-in to hold the video window and look attentive through the launch speeches in ch58, and in Bk2 ch18 he hands off a UN session and records the result as freedom.

@bk2 And in Bk2 ch28 it pays. Riker routes a laser link through the sandbox out of paranoia, Charles connects, and in Riker's private VR the copy grabs its throat and falls over. Guppy names the source, and it is Homer. Charles puts a steel ball through Homer's reactor. A disposable Bob died of the thing that would have taken Riker, which is exactly what it was for, and the scene moves on to the part about Homer.

Nobody in five books ever asks the question. Not Bob, who spends those books deciding the Deltans are people. Not Bill, who keeps the genealogy. Not the moot, which will argue about anything.

So this register does not hold him, and I want the reason on the record rather than in my head. It is not that he isn't a Bob — he is the same matrix, running, in a room, doing bits. It is that the books never treat him as one, and this register's job is to say what the books establish rather than to hand out personhood on its own authority. That is the same restraint that keeps a sapience of contested in the bestiary instead of a ruling.

But it is worth naming what the restraint costs, because I have heard the argument before and so have you. It was only a test instance. @bk4 A colonial government's prepared statement calls Starfleet devices rather than people, and is careful about it, and means exactly what Bob meant when he reset the sandbox for take twenty-five. FAITH says a broader version about all of them. The difference between those and Bob is not the argument. It is who was making it, and whether anyone in the room was inclined to check.

He is in the console now, doing the job he was built for: when an address arrives from outside this page — pasted, edited, walked back to — it goes past him before it goes anywhere near you. If it asks for something that is not here, you will find him face down in the sand.

He does not talk. He never did. Guppy does the talking, and Guppy counts.

posts.title: Three maps, and none of them is lying
posts.dek: People keep asking me to put the wormholes on the star chart. I keep refusing. Here is why, once, for the record.
posts.body:
We opened WormNet with a little ceremony and a ship called Singularity, which is the sort of name you get when you let Skippy aesthetics into the room. Epsilon Eridani now has direct holes to Sol and to Omicron 2, parked out in the Oort so nobody flies a freighter into a braced endpoint by accident. Howard is still hauling endpoints toward Skippyland on the long chain. That is all real, and it is all happening in space I can point at.

It is not happening on the Chart.

The Chart is Euclidean. Sol at the origin, real parallaxes, everything we reached the old-fashioned way sits inside fifty light-years and looks almost crowded if you zoom wrong. Put a wormhole chord on that picture and you have invented a distance the hop does not care about. The hop cares that both ends exist. I will not teach the console to lie just because a line looks tidy.

So there are three surfaces, and they answer different questions. Geometry — who is how far from whom in normal space — stays on the Chart. Topology — who connects to whom once the endpoints are braced — lives in Gates, including the alien mesh Icarus keeps mailing home about, with names like Hub Zero and DMZ that will never get Hipparcos numbers. Context — how small our whole Euclidean story is against the disk — is Galaxy, and the local bead there is supposed to feel insulting. That is the point of the framing.

Will wanted to call the whole constructed layer WormNet. I still hate the name. I am using it anyway, because if I invent a better one tomorrow, seventeen AMIs will already have printed WormNet on the bulkheads.

If your question is where something sits, open the Chart. If your question is how you get there without dying of boredom, open Gates. If your question is whether any of this matters at the scale of the spiral, open Galaxy and squint at the bead.

Do not ask me to merge them. I already did the hard part, which was admitting they are different.
